question: When Commissioner Brunner spoke at the meeting of Parliament’s Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs of 6 August 2026 about measures that need to be taken in order to enhance EU border management, he mentioned that he aims to ‘improve our prefrontier intelligence’, ‘step up Frontex’s vulnerability assessments’ and overall strengthen the support Frontex offers to non-EU countries. 1.
Exactly what improved or additional pre-frontier intelligence measures is the Commission envisaging?
In what way will the Commission step up Frontex’s vulnerability assessments?

Did the common pre-frontier intelligence picture and Eurosur framework fail either before or during the surge of irregular arrivals in Ceuta at the end of July? If so, why, and what conclusions will the Commission draw from this failure regarding binding obligations for non-EU countries on border management cooperation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.11.2026) Strengthening pre-frontier situational awareness is crucial to better anticipating and responding to the developments affecting the migratory situation in the EU.

As announced in its 5-point plan1, the Commission is working on measures to: increase cooperation with partner countries to prevent illegal migration; strengthen the EU’s external borders through a new European Emergency Response Framework and reinforce the mandate of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex); improve monitoring, situational awareness and early-warning systems by equipping Frontex with social media monitoring capabilities, reinforcing EUROSUR2 and enhancing the EU’s ability to respond to misinformation via the Global Alliance Rapid Response Initiatives3; dismantle migrant smuggling and trafficking networks through a new mandate for EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation and reinforced cooperation with online platforms; and reinforce returns by further strengthening the EU’s capacity to ensure the effective and sustainable return of persons without a right to stay.

The Commission is reflecting on how to step up Frontex’s vulnerability assessment as an important component of preparedness, to improve situational awareness, ensuring early detection of emerging risks, and fostering a resilient border management system. EUROSUR, the integrated framework for information exchange between Member States and Frontex to timely share information, is essential.

EUROSUR did not fail during the Ceuta crisis but provided an important basis for further actions undertaken by Spain in cooperation with Morocco. The new proposal for the recast European Border and Coast Guard Regulation4 envisages enhanced monitoring of EUROSUR and adequate reaction tools when a potential crisis is detected, like wider use of EUROSUR border surveillance services.

arrivals_en. 2 EUROSUR is the integrated framework for the information exchange and operational cooperation between Member States and Frontex on border management-related issues. http://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/1896/oj/eng. 3 https://www.icmpd.org/our-work/projects/global-alliance-rapid-response-initiatives-garri.

4 Regulation (EU) 2019/1896 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 November 2019 on the European Border and Coast Guard and repealing Regulations (EU) No 1052/2013 and (EU) 2016/1624, 14.11.2019, OJ L 295, p. 1-131: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52026PC1030.
